posts.post_subject: Supporting the DCG reflection fringe structure
posts.content_md:
I had a dream last night and I thought I would post it. I shall give it a try tonight in the lab.

I drempt that the way to support those refelction crosslinked fringes laying above the plane of the uncrosslinked fringes was to pre or post expose the hologram to a transmission grating, that is, two raw beams. A set of uniform fringes running perpendicular to the plane of the plate and crossecting all the reflection fringes.

What do you think?

posts.topic_title: Supporting the DCG reflection fringe structure
posts.author: JohnFP
posts.post_subject: Supporting the DCG reflection fringe structure
posts.content_md:
Well, I had to give it a try and really saw no difference. I did a regular Denisyuk. Then I did the same hologram (50 second exposure), then blocked off the object put an additional mirror in that caught light from below the plate and redirect it back to the plate to interfere with the reference tranmission style with a 20 second exposure. For the third test I just left tha additional mirror on the reference side in the entire time of 50 seconds. Thus bascially having two refernece beams, on from above the plate and one from below and the object light from the back. 

The regular hologram (overhead reference) was dim but I noticed the other hologram, the one made with the bottom reference beam was a bright as any DCG hologram I have ever made. The bottom reference beam, again was just overflow and was about half the intensity of the original referece beam. Because the angle was so great between the two reference beam, they did not bother one another, but of course the downside it the bright hologram needed to be replayed upside down.

So what happened was, not only was their additional lighting to the object through the plate but the second (bottom) reference beam had much less intensity. Thus the overall ration of object beam to bottom reference beam was lower. I know one can always add additional light to the object from the side but most of my objects are always so close to the plate this is not an option.

I may pursue this further by expanding my reference beam such the the lower intensity part falls on the plate and the higher intensity part misses the plate (below the plate) then put the mirror in at the bottom as before thus having the lower intenisty reference beam come in from the top and a more object lighting from the bottom.

posts.topic_title: Supporting the DCG reflection fringe structure
posts.author: JohnFP
posts.post_subject: Supporting the DCG reflection fringe structure
posts.content_md:
Tommy, yes, the tranmission grating is definitely there.

dcgman, I guess I am grasping for air. Do you know of any electron microscope photos of the reflection fringe structure in DCG?

What give the two different fringes different indexes of refraction? Is it the different concentration of amino chains? Or are the concentrations unaffected (no migration or loss to in water) and it is simply that one layer is heavily crosslinked and the other is not. Then I ask, what makes crosslinked gelatin have a higher index of refration then the uncrosslinked and what is happening with the greenies?

Are the greenies a collapse of fringes? A breaking of the crosslinking? What?

Maybe I am trying to overthink the problem. Maybe I should just accept that their is no gelatin loss, the fringes do not collapse, the chemical hardening is just a waste of time and accept the idea that the "springs" have been stretched past their critical point such that they no longer act like springs (whatever that means, I still don't get it). If this spring analogy is correct, how in the heck can I get greenies if all my processing temperatures are 70 degrees? Do I have to process even colder?

Do you know of any detailed papers on exactly what each step does mechanically to DCG? Maybe I just haven't found the right one yet. I do know it is not understood or there would not be so much contradiction out there. 

My final course of action will be to obtain a ph meter of some type. This is the only parameter I have not been able to monitor.

There is something I am missing. I can make two batches of emulsion exactly the same way, expose and process identially and I get different results.

Finally, if you would not mind, explain this phenomenon.

I can see two different ways that the DCG dries with the Hair Dryer. 

One is the image is dim red in the last alcohol bath, I take it out and dry it and it starts to shift to bright yellow as it dries.

The second is the image is dim red in the last alcohol bath, I take it out and dry it and it turnes very milky white with a lot of little cracks all over the whole emulsion surface. But if I continue to dry the hologram and this takes 5 to 10 minutes the white crackly surface starts to fade and out come a brilliant yellow hologram. Almost always the latter description yields a brighter and crisper hologram. 

What is actually going on different with these two observed effects?

Anyway, have a good day. Oh by the way, As I stated there is no indication that the fringes do need the added support of the tranmission grating as proposed because I still got a tiny little greenis on those too.

posts.topic_title: Supporting the DCG reflection fringe structure
posts.author: JohnFP
posts.post_subject: Supporting the DCG reflection fringe structure
posts.content_md:
This is still bothering me. I understand dcgman's reply that nothing is supporting the fringe structure but in his post he himself stated "The area in the 'uncrosslinked fringes' is mostly gel with a few vacuoles" thus implying the vacuoles (which I thought was a void filled with liquid) or air spaces are being supported by gel. 

Now looking at the difference between a very bright and efficient DCG hologram and a less efficient hologram I would have to state that there is either a higher density of gelatin in the crosslinked, exposed fringes (layers nearly horizontal to the glass plane) or a lesser density of gelatin in the uncrosslinked, unexposed fringes. I believe this to be true to a certain extent. I believe the real efficiency arises from the introduction of the gelatin matrix to remain uncollapsed in the unexposed regions and the water trapped in between that matrix to be dried out and replaced by air spaces. I may agree, I am not sure yet, that there are few of these voids but the fact remains that if the water is taken out of these spaces without the fringe structure remaining supportive the fringes collapse. This is evident in the fact that you cannot simply dry a fixed and water swelled DCG with air. It need to be dehydrated with alcohol with allows the water to be taken out while also providing support to the amino acid chains. As the alcohol is completely taken out, the amino chains remain relatively in the same place as when they were in the unprocessed emulsion.

But here is the part I don't get, still. What is it about the crosslinked sites that are different from the uncrosslinked sites? Is the water locked in by chemical bonding so that the alcohol does not replace it in the crosslinked sites? Is it that the crosslinking cages in the water? Why is the water replaced by alcohol in the uncrosslinked sites and not the crosslinked sites?

The only way I can imagine it right now is the DCG process may be a reversal process. That is, is there just a very small amount of water in the entire emulsion? Then it is exposed. The crosslinked sites are hardened in that they will not absorb any more (or very, very little) additional water. But the uncrosslinked site will absorb lots of water. The water, which is mostly in the uncrosslinked sites, is then replaced by some alcohol allowing the gelatin to remain stretched and swollen and less dense in those areas but it starts to shrink back to its original size. As the alcohol treatment continues the emulsion in that uncrosslinked site does finally get back to its original size but all the water is now been replaced by alcohol. This is evident as the hologram becomes visible in the 100% alcohol after some time. Then the final drying removed the alcohol from the uncrosslinked sites providing air spaces there. This to me seems a reversal process as it is the unexposed regions that the developing process works on, no the exposed regions.

Now again, is there still water in the crosslinked sites trapped in the gelatin or has that been dried out in the process?

Is there a higher density of gelatin in the crosslinked site compared to the uncrosslinked site? Does some get washed away in the uncrosslinked site depending on hardening amount post exposure?

Is the final thickness of one half of the fringe (either crosslinked or uncrosslinked) thicker being offset by the other half of the fringe being thinner thus a replay of the same wavelength as the recording wavelength? To explain further, I assume I can have a 488nm spacing from center of crosslinked to center of crosslinked with the uncrosslinked are in between being 244nm or 200nm or 300nm, right?

I know, leave well enought alone cause it works.

posts.content_md:
Thanks Michael, I just didn't want to sound like I was belaboring some subject. So....

It is truly fascinating to me. I would also like to know, and it seems like from what I found, is that the different bloom may indicate different amino chain lengths in the gelatin. When the collagen in processed (alkali cooked) the information I have is that if it is cooked harder and longer the triple helix of the collagen not only breaks into three amino chains that when cooling combine only partially, but each of the chains (about .3 microns long) can break into smaller pieces which then also partially combine upon cooling to the "gelatin" we know.

This is important for a number of reasons.

If the amino chains are long (.3 microns) and the chain happens to lay half in crosslinked section and half in a non crosslinked section and the emulsion is then put into water, upon drying does the half of the chain laying in the uncrosslinked section get pulled to the anchored crosslinked section, thus increasing density in that section?

Some cook at 105F some cook at 160F (at least in two papers). Does cooking at 160 break down additional amino chain into smaller chains, thus changing the bloom?

Or is bloom solely dependent on the ratios of the different types of amino acids (I think not).

Anyway, eventually I WILL find the answers I am looking for, but I thought if others were not so proud so as to admit that it is fully not understood what is going on, then a nice dialog could be forthcoming and we may collectively get a few more answers. I am sure no one fully understands what is going up just by reading the different theories and papers out their, especially from the pharmaceutical companies dumping millions into this exact research
